visual_goal: Show Keystone's sequence as a dependency roadmap: foundations first, two dated constraints pulling items forward, ledger convergence late because everything else feeds it, continuous close last.
prompt: A left-to-right roadmap across four soft vertical bands labeled at the top '2027', '2028', '2029' and '2030'; the '2028' band is the widest. Three horizontal lanes run through it. At the far left of the '2027' band a tall foundation stone labeled 'Decision rights'. Top lane: 'Group CoA v2' in 2027, then in 2028 two boxes stacked: 'ViDA' with a small red calendar flag reading '1 July 2028', and below it 'Canonical events'. Middle lane: 'Payments to ledger' in 2027, then directly to its right in 2028 the box 'Merchant invoicing', at the same height. Bottom lane: 'Wave 0' in 2027, then in 2028 'Wave 1', then still inside the 2028 band a box 'Colocation ends' with a small red calendar flag reading '31 Dec 2028'. In the '2029' band one large box 'Ledger convergence' at middle height. In the '2030' band a box 'Continuous close' with a circular arrow icon. Every arrow is a separate line with its own arrowhead; no lines merge. Arrows: from 'Decision rights' one arrow each into 'Group CoA v2', 'Payments to ledger' and 'Wave 0'; from 'Group CoA v2' one arrow into 'ViDA', one into 'Canonical events', and one diagonal arrow down into 'Merchant invoicing'; one short straight arrow from 'Payments to ledger' into 'Merchant invoicing'; 'Wave 0' arrow into 'Wave 1', 'Wave 1' arrow into 'Colocation ends'; one arrow from 'Canonical events' and one from 'Merchant invoicing' into 'Ledger convergence'; one arrow from 'Ledger convergence' into 'Continuous close'. Exactly twelve arrows; 'Payments to ledger' has exactly one outgoing arrow, into 'Merchant invoicing'. The two red calendar flags stand out as fixed external dates.
alt: A roadmap from 2027 to 2030: decision rights first, then CoA v2, payments to ledger and wave 0; in 2028 ViDA and the colocation end as dated constraints, canonical events and merchant invoicing; ledger convergence in 2029 and continuous close last.

visual_goal: Show three separate authorities under one steering committee: PMO for plan and cost, design authority for the template and variations, benefits review for the money, with workstreams taking design questions to the design authority.
prompt: A top-down organization illustration. At the top a small boardroom table labeled 'Board', with one arrow down into a wide meeting table labeled 'Steering committee'. Below the steering committee three pillars side by side, each receiving one arrow from it: on the left 'PMO' with a calendar-chart and calculator icon; in the middle 'Design authority' with a blueprint icon; on the right 'Benefits review' with a stack of coins icon. Under 'PMO' a row of six small identical boxes grouped on one panel labeled once 'Workstreams', with one arrow from 'PMO' down to the group. From the 'Workstreams' group one curved orange arrow labeled 'design questions' rises into 'Design authority'. Below 'Design authority' an open register book labeled 'Template' with one arrow from the design authority into it. To the right of 'Design authority', between it and the benefits pillar, two small boxes each sending one arrow into the design authority: 'Review board' on top and 'Internal controls' with a shield icon below. Exactly nine arrows.
alt: Board above a steering committee, which oversees three pillars: the PMO with six workstreams, the design authority holding the template and taking advice from the review board and internal controls, and the benefits review; workstreams send design questions to the design authority.

visual_goal: Show the design authority's gap rule as a sorting line: each gap passes gates in order, and each gate has one allowed outcome, ending in refusal; custom code in the ERP core is not an outcome.
prompt: A left-to-right sorting line drawn as a conveyor belt. At the far left a puzzle piece with a missing notch rides onto the belt. The belt passes five gates in order, each gate a small arch with a short question label: 'Standard fits?', then 'Regulation?', then 'Key control?', then 'Funded differentiation?', then 'Cheap preference?'. Under each gate one green arrow drops down into one outcome tray: under 'Standard fits?' a tray 'Configure'; under 'Regulation?' a tray 'Localization'; under 'Key control?' a tray 'Template change'; under 'Funded differentiation?' a tray 'Outside the core', drawn as a small service box sitting outside a large sealed box; under 'Cheap preference?' a tray 'Dated variation' with a small hourglass. After the last gate the belt ends at a grey bin labeled 'Refused'. Exactly five green arrows plus the belt.
alt: A conveyor carrying a gap through five gates: standard fit leads to configure, regulation to localization, key control to template change, funded differentiation to a service outside the core, cheap preference to a dated variation, and everything else is refused.
